opus-5.5.text:
I think this is the question I get asked most, and honestly it's one I think about a lot myself.

My view is that mathematics was never only about producing a proof and stamping "QED" at the bottom. A proof is an artifact, but the real thing mathematicians care about is understanding: why something is true, how it connects to other ideas, what it opens up. If an AI system hands you a ten-thousand-line verified proof of some conjecture, that's wonderful, because now we *know* it's true. But in many ways the human work starts there. What's the key idea? Can we compress it? Does it suggest a new definition or a new framework? Those questions don't go away; they become more central.

There's a historical parallel I like. When computers started doing large calculations, or when the four color theorem was proved with computer assistance, people worried this was the end of something. Instead, mathematicians absorbed it, argued about it, and eventually asked deeper questions. I expect something similar here, just at a much larger scale and faster pace.

I also think the role of the mathematician shifts somewhat toward taste and direction. Deciding which problems matter, which conjectures are worth stating, what counts as a beautiful or illuminating result: that's a deeply human judgment, shaped by culture and by what we find meaningful. AI can explore an enormous space, but someone has to say "this corner is interesting, go look here," and then interpret what comes back.

And there's a very practical side. Formal verification tools like Lean, combined with AI, could take away a lot of the tedium: checking cases, filling in routine lemmas, catching errors in a long paper that a referee might miss. That frees people to spend more time on the creative part. Young mathematicians especially might get to do research earlier, because the barrier of mastering every technical detail before you can contribute becomes lower.

So I'm actually optimistic. I don't think the intellectual life of mathematicians disappears. I think it becomes more like having an incredibly capable collaborator. The joy of understanding something, that moment where it clicks, is not something you can outsource. You still have to have it yourself. And as long as people want that experience, mathematics as a human activity will continue.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians will choose meaningful problems and direct AI toward interesting areas, but it does not say they will create problems that stump AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. I think about this a lot, because I came into mathematics for a very specific kind of pleasure, and I want to be honest about what AI changes and what it doesn't.

Let me start with what mathematics actually is for the people who do it. Most people imagine it's about getting the right answer. But when you sit in a seminar room at Princeton or MIT, nobody is excited about an answer. They're excited about a reason. A proof that works but gives you no understanding is considered almost a disappointment. People say, "Okay, it's true, but why is it true?" That question, "why," is the center of mathematical life. And I don't think that goes away just because a machine can produce a verified proof.

What AI is already changing is the economics of attention. For a long time, a mathematician's time was spent on a lot of work that was not really the creative part. Checking a lemma. Searching for whether something was already known in a 1970s paper written in Russian. Trying twenty small variations of an argument until one closes. A lot of this is now becoming cheap. And when something becomes cheap, people stop measuring their worth by it.

I think this is actually a return to an older idea of the mathematician. If you look at someone like Poincaré or Hilbert, they weren't primarily grinders. They were people who decided what questions mattered. They built frameworks that made whole areas visible. Taste, in other words. And taste is the thing that is hardest to automate, because taste is about deciding what is worth caring about, and that depends on what humans find beautiful and meaningful, not on what is formally derivable.

So in the near term, I think the mathematician's intellectual life shifts toward three things. First, asking questions. Choosing the right definition, the right conjecture, the right level of generality. Second, interpretation. When a system produces a proof that is five thousand lines long, someone has to understand it, compress it, and connect it to the rest of human knowledge. Reading will become as important as writing. Third, judgment about what is important. There are infinitely many true statements. Almost all of them are boring. Deciding which ones deserve a name is a deeply human act.

I also want to be careful not to be too romantic. There is a real loss. Some mathematicians got their joy from exactly the kind of hard, slow technical struggle that AI will shortcut. Working for three years on a problem and then having the moment where it opens up. If a model can do that in an afternoon, some people will feel that the thing they loved has been taken from them. I think we should be honest about that grief rather than pretending everything is only an upgrade.

But here is what gives me hope. In chess, when computers surpassed humans, people predicted chess would die. Instead, more people play chess now than at any point in history. The engines didn't end chess, they changed what it means to be good at it. Players study with engines and develop a kind of understanding that didn't exist before. I think mathematics may go the same way. Working alongside systems that can explore enormous spaces of ideas may give humans a kind of mathematical intuition we have never had access to.

And finally, I'd say the social life of mathematics continues. Mathematics has always been a conversation across generations. Fermat writes something in a margin, and people talk to him for three hundred years. AI becomes a new participant in that conversation, maybe a very productive one, but it doesn't replace the fact that humans want to explain things to each other, argue about what matters, and feel wonder together. That part, the wonder, is not a bottleneck that needs to be optimized away. It's the point.

r001.rationale: The response says mathematicians will choose questions, definitions, and conjectures, but does not say they will create problems intended to stump AI.

astra-6.text:
I think mathematicians’ intellectual lives will change, but I don’t think they’ll disappear. There’s a difference between getting an answer to a mathematical question and understanding why that answer is true, how it connects to other ideas, and what questions it opens up next.

Even if AI becomes very good at proving theorems, there’s still the question of what we find interesting. Which definitions help us see something we couldn’t see before? Which problems are worth spending years thinking about? AI could participate in those decisions too, so I wouldn’t draw a permanent boundary around some activity and say, “Only humans can do this.”

But intellectual life isn’t valuable only because you can do something nobody else can do. You can learn a beautiful piece of mathematics that thousands of people already understand, and the experience can still transform how you think. That doesn’t go away because a machine understands it too.

My hope is that AI gives more people access to that experience: a collaborator that helps you get unstuck, explore examples, and follow an intuition further. The challenge is making sure we use it in ways that deepen our understanding, because having a proof available isn’t the same as having made sense of it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses choosing worthwhile problems and allows that AI may participate in those decisions, but it does not propose that mathematicians will create problems that stump AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I think mathematicians’ intellectual lives will change, but I don’t think they’ll disappear. A lot of the pleasure of mathematics comes from understanding why something is true, not simply knowing that it is true. Even if an AI can give you a proof, there’s still a very personal process of making that proof your own—seeing the idea behind it, connecting it to something else, figuring out what it opens up.

And if AI makes certain kinds of problem-solving much easier, then choosing the questions becomes more important. What’s worth understanding? Which definitions reveal something interesting? Where is there a connection that we haven’t yet learned to articulate? Those are mathematical activities, too.

I wouldn’t want to assume that those activities will always be beyond AI. But I also don’t think their value depends on humans being uniquely capable of them. We can still find meaning in thinking deeply, learning from one another, and discovering something for ourselves, even in a world where a machine could have reached it first.

r001.rationale: The response says choosing questions will matter more, but does not propose that mathematicians will create problems that stump AI; it explicitly avoids assuming those activities will remain beyond AI.
